extra_qs.q: What is arr after this call, and what does partition return?
extra_qs.c:
arr = [4, 7, 2, 6, 5]
pos = partition(arr, 0, 4)    # Lomuto, last element is the pivot
extra_qs.e: Pivot 5. Only 4 and 2 are ≤ 5, so they are swapped into slots 0 and 1 in the order they are met: [4, 2, 7, 6, 5]. Then the pivot swaps with slot 2. The values right of the pivot are not sorted, just bigger.

extra_qs.q: What does the max-heap array look like after this insert?
extra_qs.e: 10 goes to index 5. Its parent is (5 − 1) // 2 = 2, holding 8: swap. Now at index 2, the parent is index 0 holding 9: swap again. 10 is the new root.

extra_qs.q: What does delete_max return, and what is left in the heap?
extra_qs.e: The last value 8 moves to the root: [8, 7, 9, 3, 5]. Sift down: the children are 7 and 9, so swap with the larger, 9. At index 2 there are no children left, so it stops.

extra_qs.q: Insert these keys into an empty BST, in this order. What is the preorder traversal?
extra_qs.c:
for k in [50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60]:
    root = insert(root, k)
extra_qs.e: Preorder visits the node, then the whole left subtree, then the right. The sorted list is inorder; 20 40 30 60 70 50 is postorder; 50 30 70 20 40 60 is level order.

extra_qs.q: What does recursive DFS print, starting from 0?
extra_qs.e: From 0 go to 1 first, from 1 to 3. Vertex 3 has no outgoing edges, so back out to 0 and try 2. Its neighbour 3 is already visited. 0 1 2 3 would be the BFS order.

extra_qs.q: What order does BFS process the vertices in, starting from 0?
extra_qs.e: Neighbours are queued in list order: 0 queues 2 then 1. Processing 2 queues 4; processing 1 queues 3. The queue is first in, first out, so 4 comes before 3. 0 2 4 1 3 is the DFS order.

extra_qs.q: What does subsets([1, 2]) return, with "exclude" tried before "include"?
extra_qs.c:
def go(i):
    if i == len(nums):
        res.append(cur[:]); return
    go(i + 1)                # exclude nums[i]
    cur.append(nums[i])      # include it
    go(i + 1)
    cur.pop()
extra_qs.e: The deepest decision (about 2) flips fastest. Exclude 1 then exclude 2 gives []; exclude 1, include 2 gives [2]; then the include-1 branch gives [1] and [1, 2]. [[], [], [], []] is what you get if you forget the [:] copy.

extra_qs.q: What is the time complexity of this code?
extra_qs.e: The outer loop runs n times. The inner loop doubles j until it reaches i, about log₂ i times. The sum of log i for i up to n is Θ(n log n).

extra_qs.q: What does rob([2, 7, 9, 3, 1]) return?
extra_qs.e: dp = [2, 7, 11, 11, 12]. Robbing houses 0, 2 and 4 gives 2 + 9 + 1 = 12. Greedily taking 7 and 3 gives only 10.

extra_qs.q: 0/1 knapsack with weights [1, 3, 4], values [15, 20, 30], capacity 4. What is dp[n][W]?
extra_qs.e: Items 1 and 3 together weigh exactly 4 and are worth 15 + 20 = 35, which beats item 4 alone (30). 50 and 65 would need a total weight above 4.

extra_qs.q: What does Kahn’s algorithm return for this graph? (Vertices with in-degree 0 are queued in index order.)
extra_qs.e: Vertices 0 and 1 start at in-degree 0 and are popped in that order. Vertex 2 reaches in-degree 0 only after both are gone, then 3.

extra_qs.q: What distances does Dijkstra return from vertex 0?
extra_qs.e: 0 → 2 → 1 costs 1 + 2 = 3, which beats the direct edge 0 → 1 of cost 4.

extra_qs.q: Edge weights are all 0 or 1. Which algorithm runs in O(V + E)?
extra_qs.e: Free edges push to the front of the deque and cost-1 edges to the back, so the deque stays sorted by distance without a heap.

extra_qs.q: Why does the textbook Dijkstra fail on a graph with a negative edge?
o: A vertex finalised early can later be undercut
extra_qs.e: On 0→1 (2), 0→2 (3), 2→1 (−2) the textbook version finalises vertex 1 at 2, but 0→2→1 costs 1.

extra_qs.q: A graph has 6 vertices and no negative cycle. How many rounds of Bellman–Ford are always enough?
extra_qs.e: A shortest simple path has at most V − 1 = 5 edges.

extra_qs.q: What does this “at most k stops” search return (k = 1 stop, so up to 2 edges)?
extra_qs.e: One stop allows 0 → 1 → 2 for 100 + 100 = 200, which beats the direct flight at 500.

extra_qs.q: What total weight does Kruskal return?
extra_qs.e: Kept in order: 1, 3, 4. The edges of weight 5 and 6 would each close a cycle.

extra_qs.q: Why is Kruskal’s running time O(E log E)?
o: Sorting the edges dominates; union-find is almost constant per operation
Each edge needs a full DFS
It builds an E × E table
extra_qs.e: After the sort, each edge costs one find or union, which is near-constant with path compression and union by size.

extra_qs.q: Course Schedule (LC 207): prerequisites [[1, 0]] means…
o: take course 0 before course 1, so the edge is 0 → 1
extra_qs.e: The pair is [a, b]: to take a you must first take b, so the edge points from b to a.

extra_qs.q: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix (LC 329) is solved with Kahn’s algorithm by counting…
o: the number of BFS layers peeled
extra_qs.e: Each layer adds one more cell to the longest path; peeling avoids the deep recursion the memoised DFS needs.

extra_qs.q: Path With Maximum Probability (LC 1514) with heapq: what do you push?
o: the negated probability, because heapq is a min-heap
extra_qs.e: Popping the smallest negated value pops the largest probability.

extra_qs.q: Which statement is the cycle property of MSTs?
o: An edge strictly heavier than every other edge on some cycle belongs to no MST
Every cycle contains an MST edge
The lightest edge of a cycle is never in an MST
MSTs contain no cycles, so cycles are irrelevant
extra_qs.e: Swap it out for the cycle’s lighter edges and the tree gets lighter, so it cannot have been minimum.

extra_qs.q: Which algorithm answers “connect all 3,000 points in the plane at minimum total distance”?
o: Prim without a heap, O(n²), on the implicit complete graph
extra_qs.e: The graph is complete (about 4.5 million edges), so the array version of Prim beats sorting all edges.

extra_qs.q: What do greedy and the DP return for coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6?
extra_qs.e: Greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins; the best is 3 + 3 = 2 coins.

extra_qs.q: What does Task Scheduler return?
extra_qs.e: A B _ A B _ A B: the frame is (3 − 1) · (2 + 1) = 6 plus a final row holding the 2 tasks tied for the highest count.

extra_qs.q: What does Partition Labels return?
extra_qs.e: The first piece ends at the last “a” (index 8), the second at the last “e” (index 15), the third is the rest.

extra_qs.q: What does Jump Game (LC 55) return?
o: it depends on the order of jumps
extra_qs.e: Every route lands on index 3, whose jump length is 0, so index 4 is out of reach.

extra_qs.q: For which problem is “take the highest value per kilo first” provably optimal?
extra_qs.e: Only when fractions are allowed can no capacity be stranded.

extra_qs.q: What does this return? (index of the next strictly greater element, −1 if none)
extra_qs.e: Both 2s see the 4 at index 3 first as strictly greater; the 1 sees the 2 at index 2.

extra_qs.q: The code uses a strict comparison. What does it return when values are equal?
extra_qs.e: Equal values are not greater, so the first 2 must wait for the 3 at index 2, exactly like the second 2.

extra_qs.q: Why is a monotonic stack pass O(n) even though one step may pop many elements?
o: each element is pushed once and popped at most once
extra_qs.e: The total number of pops cannot exceed the total number of pushes: that is amortised analysis.

extra_qs.q: What does the one-row version return?
extra_qs.e: The longest common subsequence is “ace”, length 3.

extra_qs.q: Why does the one-row LCS need a saved “diag” variable?
o: The cell diagonal to you is overwritten before you need it
extra_qs.e: dp[i][j] reads dp[i+1][j+1], which lives in the slot that was just overwritten for the previous j.

extra_qs.q: A table cell reads only the cell above and the cell to its left. Which way do the loops run?
o: forwards in both i and j
extra_qs.e: Both dependencies have smaller indices, so they must be filled first.

extra_qs.q: What does House Robber III return for the tree [3, 2, 3, null, 3, null, 1]?
extra_qs.e: Rob the root (3) and the two grandchildren (3 and 1): 3 + 3 + 1 = 7. Robbing the two middle nodes gives 2 + 3 = 5.

extra_qs.q: After adding 5, 2 and 8 to the two-heap median finder, what is find_median()?
extra_qs.c:
m = MedianFinder()
for x in (5, 2, 8):
    m.add_num(x)
print(m.find_median())
extra_qs.e: Sorted: 2, 5, 8; the middle is 5. The max-heap holds {2, 5} with top 5; the min-heap holds {8}.

blanks.p: Lomuto partition: the last element is the pivot, k marks the end of the "≤ pivot" zone.
The recursive driver: stop at 0 or 1 element, and never include the pivot in either half.
Recursive BST insert that re-attaches whatever comes back.
Inorder traversal: the one that lists a BST in sorted order.
The two-children delete case: copy up the inorder successor, then remove it.
Index arithmetic for a heap stored in a 0-based array.
Insert into a max-heap: add at the end, then bubble up.
Sift down: swap with the LARGER child until the order rule holds.
Build a heap in O(n): sift down every parent, from the last one back to the root.
All subsets: exclude, include, undo. Save a copy, not the live list.
blanks.c:
def subsets(nums):
    res, cur = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == {{len(nums)}}:
            res.append(cur{{[:]|.copy()}})
            return
        go(i + 1)
        cur.{{append}}(nums[i])
        go(i + 1)
        cur.{{pop}}()
    go(0)
    return res

blanks.p: Permutations: two things change on CHOOSE, so two things are restored on UNDO.
Recursive DFS: mark on entry, recurse into unvisited neighbours.
BFS with a deque. Mark a vertex the moment you enqueue it.
Climbing Stairs, bottom-up.
House Robber: skip house i, or rob it and add the best up to i − 2.
The LCS cell rule.
0/1 Knapsack: skip item i, or take it if it fits.
Master theorem for T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n), with c = log_b(a). Write the answers with ^ for powers.
blanks.c:
f(n) polynomially smaller than n^c  ->  T(n) = Θ({{n^c}})
f(n) = Θ(n^c)                       ->  T(n) = Θ({{n^c log n|n^c·log n|n^c * log n|n^c lg n}})
f(n) polynomially larger than n^c   ->  T(n) = Θ({{f(n)}})

Reader–writer partition: move every even number to the front.
Build an R × C grid of zeros with R separate rows.

blanks.p: Memoize a recursive function with the standard library.
Multi-source BFS: one whole level of the queue per minute.
Frog Jump, bottom-up: the last jump came from i − 1 or i − 2.
Keep the most non-overlapping intervals.
Dijkstra with lazy deletion: skip stale pairs, relax with the popped distance.
Kahn: queue a vertex the moment its last prerequisite is done.
0/1 knapsack in one row: the capacity loop runs downward.
Kahn’s algorithm: peel every vertex whose prerequisites are all done.
Dijkstra with a heap: skip stale entries, relax, push the improvement.
Kruskal: lightest edges first, keep an edge only if it joins two components.
At most k stops: k + 1 rounds, each reading the OLD distances.
Next strictly greater element: pop everything smaller than the newcomer.
Most non-overlapping intervals: sort by END time, keep what starts after the last kept one ends.
One-row LCS: save the diagonal before it is overwritten.

bugs.p: Deleting a node with two children breaks the BST rule.
bugs.e: The inorder successor is the smallest value in the RIGHT subtree. The smallest value on the left is smaller than the rest of the left subtree, so copying it up breaks the rule, and line 15 then tries to delete a value that is not on the right at all.
bugs.f: succ = find_min(node.right)

bugs.p: After some inserts, a child is bigger than its parent.
bugs.e: i // 2 is the parent formula for 1-based arrays. With 0-based Python lists the parent of i is (i − 1) // 2: for i = 2, i // 2 gives 1, but the real parent is 0.
bugs.f: parent = (i - 1) // 2

bugs.p: delete_max returns the right value, but the heap left behind is sometimes invalid.

if r < n and heap[r] > heap[i]: big = r
bugs.e: The right child must be compared with heap[big], the larger of the parent and the left child. Comparing with heap[i] picks the right child whenever it beats the parent, even when the left child is larger, so the smaller child is promoted above its bigger sibling.

bugs.p: subsets([1, 2]) returns [[], [], [], []] instead of four different subsets.
bugs.e: res stores four references to the same list. Every undo empties it again, so by the end all four entries show []. Save a snapshot with cur[:].
bugs.f: res.append(cur[:])      # save a copy

bugs.p: permute(0, [], [False] * 4, 3) prints [1, 2, 3] and nothing else.
bugs.e: CHOOSE changed two things, so UNDO must restore two things. Leaving visited[num] as True means every number stays "used" after the first branch, and no other arrangement can be built.
bugs.f: visited[num] = False    # undo BOTH changes

bugs.p: With adj = [[1, 2, 3], [0], [0], [0]] this "BFS" returns [0, 3, 2, 1] instead of [0, 1, 2, 3].
bugs.e: pop() removes from the right: last in, first out. That turns the queue into a stack and the search into a DFS-like order. BFS takes the oldest vertex with popleft().
bugs.f: node = queue.popleft()    # first in, first out

bugs.p: dfs(0, ...) on an undirected graph crashes with RecursionError.
bugs.e: The node is only marked after all its neighbours are explored. In an undirected graph 0 sees 1, 1 sees 0 (still unmarked), 0 sees 1 again, and so on. Mark on entry, before the loop.

bugs.p: ways_table(4) raises IndexError instead of returning 5.
bugs.e: The answer lives in dp[n], so the table needs indices 0 to n: that is n + 1 slots.
bugs.f: dp = [1] * (n + 1)      # indices 0..n

bugs.p: ways_memo(40, {}) takes minutes, as slow as plain recursion.

parsons.p: Order the lines of partition (last element is the pivot).
parsons.why: Grow the zone (k += 1) before swapping into it, and only place the pivot after the scan, at k + 1.

parsons.p: Order the lines so every reachable vertex is visited exactly once.
parsons.why: Mark on entry, before the loop. Marking afterwards lets a neighbour call straight back into this node and recurse forever.

parsons.p: Order the lines of BFS that records the distance (in edges) from start.
parsons.why: dist doubles as the visited array: −1 means "not reached". Set a vertex's distance the moment it is discovered, from the vertex that discovered it. The queue setup and the last two lines can swap without changing the result.

parsons.p: Order the lines that count connected components using dfs from the puzzle above.
parsons.why: Each time the outer loop finds an unvisited vertex, a brand new component starts there; one dfs call then marks the whole component.

parsons.p: Order the lines of delete_max for a max-heap stored in a list.
parsons.why: Read the root before touching the list: with a one-item heap, pop() empties it and heap[0] would fail. Then the last value fills the root and sinks to its place.

parsons.p: Order the lines of the include / exclude backtracking for subsets.
parsons.why: The base case saves a copy and returns. Then: one branch without nums[i], one with it, and an undo straight after the "with" branch. Trying "include" first is also correct; it only changes the output order.
Create the table with the base cases filled, fill it from small i to large, then read the answer from dp[n].

parsons.p: Order the loops and the cell rule that fill the LCS table c.
parsons.why: Row by row, left to right, so the three cells each entry reads (diagonal, above, left) are already filled. The indentation tells you which loop is outer.

parsons.p: Order the lines of the iterative reverse.
parsons.why: Save the rest of the list before turning the arrow; move prev up to cur before cur moves on; the old tail (prev) is the new head.

parsons.p: Order the lines of the topological sort that detects cycles.
c: q = deque(u for u in range(n) if indeg[u] == 0)
return order if len(order) == n else None
parsons.why: Count in-degrees first, queue the sources, then pop, record, lower the neighbours’ counts and queue those that reach zero. The final length check is what reports a cycle.

parsons.p: Order the lines of Dijkstra (stale-entry check included).
c: for u, v, w in edges:
parsons.why: Pop first, skip the stale entry, and only then relax; a push happens only when a strictly shorter route is found.

parsons.p: Order the lines of Kruskal’s MST.
c: for w, u, v in sorted(edges):
return total if used == n - 1 else None
parsons.why: Sort first so the lightest edge is considered first; add the weight only when union() accepts the edge; check V − 1 edges at the end.

parsons.p: Order the lines of the monotonic-stack scan.
parsons.why: For each newcomer, first answer everyone on the stack it beats, then push the newcomer itself.
